doc.title: Phoebe Jacobs and Jackie Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

chapter: Youth, war and the Armstrong club
title: World War II, Eubie Blake and musicians' patriotism
summary: Jacobs describes Armstrong, Ellington and Eubie Blake entertaining troops despite segregation, and Blake's song 'We Are Americans Too'.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: This is a little off the subject but how did the second World War affect the lives of musicians? Were you able to observe any of that?

Well the thing that I got out of the second World War was an awareness of what my heroes were doing that were here in America. Eubie Blake went to over 900 USO camps. Now I’m talking about a man whose mother and father were slaves and he never got a penny from the United States government but he had the calling and the need to go entertain his troops. Louis went, Duke went, I mean the greatest thing that these men had was their pride in their country.
Did it surprise you that more of them did not turn out to be bitter with that kind of treatment?

Well again I’ve got to go back to Eubie. Because Eubie wrote a song during World War I, I don’t know if you’re aware about it, of the fact that the United States Army was segregated. And he went to Paris with James Reese Europe in 1919 or 1920 I believe. And he visited hospitals there and he watched a black soldier giving a blood transfusion to a white soldier. That’s when he was tempted to write this song which he wrote, called “We Are Americans Too” which was so illustrious of what people like Eubie felt. And he never had any anger. He said, “Look if we’re going to make it, we’ve got to do it with love for our fellow man.”
